So the way I understand Bayes is that there are certain 'stochastic' processes where there's too much detail to have a full understanding of ground truth. E.g., there are too many atoms in the dice, too many ways gene variation can manifest, too many positions the electron can be in, too many neurons in too many brains reacting to too many natural and socialogical phenomena, etc.

We cope with it as best we can. When making a prediction about the outcome of such a process, we make our best educated guess based on our experience to date. If we don't have much experience with the process, we'll have low confidence. As we interact with the process and collect data, Bayes provides a formula for updating our best guess and also measuring our confidence as it increases. The numbers we plug into the formula are just a count of the observations we've made to date.

Our 'best guess' usually means our guess for the average or 'mean' value of the process represented by the Greek letter mu. If the process is detailed enough, we're going to be wrong a fair amount of the time but having a good guess means our predictions will rarely be far off. This is what the 'maximum likelihood' means. E.g., if we're trying to predict the height of randomly selected professional basketball players, a guess of 6' 2" will be less wrong than a guess of 5' 6". Some few players will be closer to the shorter height but most will be closer to the taller height. The exact mean of all the players you've observed to date is the best guess and your expectation of the maximum likelihood.

Confidence is measured with the 'standard deviation' or ~average distance from the average~ and is represented with a lower-case sigma (upper case usually means Summation). It's also a measure of your guess about the 'variance' of the process. If the players have lots of different heights, it'll be harder to make good predictions than if the players you've seen are all about the same height.
